narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 58% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year class ranking. Placing in the second decile is substantially lower than the average of nearly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. This weak academic standing in later law school years strongly pushed the prediction toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 34 was the second most important factor. While this score is below the 37.2 average of accepted students, it actually worked in your favor and pulled the prediction slightly toward passing. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.6 had a similar but smaller positive effect; however, it too sits well below the 3.23 average of successful applicants.

In short, although your test scores offered some counter-balance, your low class ranking in year three was the dominant reason the model concluded you were more likely than not to fail the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Improving these two areas would most effectively increase your chances of admission in a future application cycle. (218 words)
